historical_basis.quote: In Scandinavian folklore, the mylingar were the phantasmal incarnations of the souls of children that had been forced to roam the earth until they could persuade someone (or otherwise cause enough of a ruckus to make their wishes known) to bury them properly.

statement.id: Dalam cerita rakyat Skandinavia, mylingar adalah penjelmaan arwah anak-anak yang terpaksa berkeliaran di bumi sampai bisa membujuk seseorang untuk menguburkan mereka dengan layak.
statement.en: In Scandinavian folklore mylingar were the phantasmal forms of children's souls forced to roam the earth until they could persuade someone to bury them properly.

historical_basis.quote: The myling (also known as utburd in Norwegian, útburður in Icelandic and ihtiriekko and liekkiö in Finnish) is said to chase lone wanderers at night and jump on their backs, demanding to be carried to the graveyard ... apparently grow heavier as they near the graveyard ... If one should prove unable to make it into the cemetery, the myling kills its victim in a rage.

statement.id: Myling (juga utburd di Norwegia, útburður di Islandia, ihtiriekko dan liekkiö di Finlandia) konon mengejar pengembara yang sendirian di malam hari, melompat ke punggungnya dan meminta dibawa ke pemakaman; ia makin berat saat mendekati pemakaman, dan bila korban gagal mencapainya, myling membunuhnya dengan murka.
statement.en: The myling (also utburd in Norwegian, útburður in Icelandic, ihtiriekko and liekkiö in Finnish) is said to chase lone wanderers at night, jump on their backs and demand to be carried to the graveyard; it grows heavier as the graveyard nears, and if the victim fails to reach it, kills them in rage.

presentation_revision_history.prompt: One square premium painterly folklore encyclopedia illustration of MYLING in the documented Norwegian UTBURD animal manifestation: ONE hornless sheep-shaped spirit by an abandoned barn at night. It is entirely sheep, no human infant face or body: one sheep head with narrow animal muzzle, two natural ears, two eyes, woolly quadruped body, exactly FOUR legs ending in four cloven hooves, one short sheep tail. Make all four legs separately visible and full body and tail comfortably framed. Walnut-grey wool, antique-gold moonlight on face, dark forest-green pasture plants and weathered barn wood; distant wooded path hints at the way to consecrated ground. The sheep stands motionless looking toward the path with a quiet insistent searching gaze, a mournful restless spirit awaiting recognition and proper burial, neither cute pet nor malicious demonic creature. Refined textured painterly realism and rich earthy mythological field-guide quality. No child or human, no wounds, blood, corpse, gravestone letters, glowing red eyes, horns, wings, extra limbs, costume, collar, magical symbols, text, watermark or border. This is the child spirit's documented sheep-form appearance, not a sheep companion.
